html:
Chilli peppers reached India in the 16th century, carried by Portuguese ships from the Americas, and changed the way most of the subcontinent cooks.

Chillies were first grown in Mexico and South America thousands of years ago. Columbus brought them to Spain in 1493, part of the Columbian Exchange. The Portuguese, who held Goa from 1510, carried them on to India.

Before then, heat in Indian food came from black pepper, long pepper, ginger and mustard. Chilli was easier: it grows almost anywhere, is cheap and adds bite and colour at once. Within a few generations it was a staple from Kerala to Kashmir.

From India and the Portuguese trade it spread on into Southeast Asia, Sichuan in China and Korea, whose kimchi turned red only after the chilli came.

Today India grows, eats and exports more chillies than any other country. It is a plain example of how food that seems ancient and local can be quite new.
sum: Chilli peppers reached India in the 16th century, carried by Portuguese ships from the Americas, and changed the way most of the subcontinent cooks.
